item.title: FTUC attacks foreign worker rule changes
item.description: THE Fiji Trades Union Congress has launched a blistering attack on Government’s decision to temporarily ease immigration requirements for employers bringing foreign workers into Fiji, warning the move could come at the expense of local jobs and workers’ rights. FTUC says the changes, which include waivers on proving that workers are unavailable locally and requirements for skills understudy, were
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Trades Union Congress has launched a blistering attack on Government’s decision to temporarily ease immigration requirements for employers bringing foreign workers into Fiji, warning the move could come at the expense of local jobs and workers’ rights.

FTUC says the changes, which include waivers on proving that workers are unavailable locally and requirements for skills understudy, were made without consultation or studies on their impact.

The union claims employers are increasingly turning to foreign workers because they can be made to work longer hours without overtime payments or other employment benefits.

FTUC general secretary Felix Anthony said the lack of oversight over foreign workers was particularly concerning, alleging some were living in poor and “unfit” conditions while facing exploitation with limited avenues for redress.

The union also questioned whether Government agencies have enough resources to monitor work permits, employment conditions, contracts and visa expiry dates amid the growing influx of foreign workers.

FTUC said the decision appeared “ad-hoc” and accused the Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation of successfully lobbying for the changes without adequate consultation with workers’ representatives.

While acknowledging that some industries require overseas labour, FTUC is calling for tripartite consultations involving Government, employers and workers before further decisions are made.

It warned that prioritising foreign labour without safeguards could undermine decent employment opportunities for Fijians and push more locals to seek work overseas.

item.title: Minor electoral breaches should not be criminalised, says CDD
item.description: THE Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 introduces penalties for conduct that should not necessarily be treated as criminal offences, according to Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD). CDD chief executive officer Nilesh Lal told the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights that Parliament should instead establish three categories of electoral offences, separating minor administrative bre
item.content:encoded:
THE Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 introduces penalties for conduct that should not necessarily be treated as criminal offences, according to Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD).

CDD chief executive officer Nilesh Lal told the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights that Parliament should instead establish three categories of electoral offences, separating minor administrative breaches from conduct that threatens the integrity of elections.

Mr Lal said the proposed legislation’s two categories, illegal electoral practice and corrupt electoral practice, were an improvement but did not go far enough.

He recommended a third category for administrative infringements, covering matters such as late filing, minor labelling errors, correctable form defects and other low-harm procedural breaches.

“These should ordinarily attract a warning, a direction to correct the issue, or a modest administrative or civil penalty, with no imprisonment,” Mr Lal said.

“The second category, illegal electoral practice, would cover deliberate or repeated breaches of electoral rules that cause genuine regulatory harm.

“The most serious category, corrupt electoral practices, should be reserved for conduct such as bribery, treating, undue influence, personation, ballot tampering and serious misuse of State resources.”

Mr Lal said the current system treated fundamentally different conduct through the same criminal lens, with severe penalties applying to technical or administrative failures.

He said an administrative mistake should not be treated in the same way as bribery or deliberate interference with an election.

CDD also raised concerns over what it described as extraordinary powers given to election administration, restrictions on civil society and research, and limits on political expression and public debate.

“CDD is not seeking to dismantle the electoral legislation, but asking Parliament to preserve what works, liberalise unnecessary restrictions and correct poorly drafted provisions.”

item.title: Recuse, don’t step down, says Lal
item.description: THE Supervisor of Elections should recuse themselves from a decision where a conflict of interest arises, rather than step down from office, the Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) says. CDD chief executive officer Nilesh Lal made the comments in relation to Clause 4 of the Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026, which deals with conflicts of interest under Section 13 of the Electoral Act 2014.
item.content:encoded:
THE Supervisor of Elections should recuse themselves from a decision where a conflict of interest arises, rather than step down from office, the Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) says.

CDD chief executive officer Nilesh Lal made the comments in relation to Clause 4 of the Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026, which deals with conflicts of interest under Section 13 of the Electoral Act 2014.

“The Bill proposes that a person would step down from his or her office for the purpose of the decision,” Mr Lal said.

Mr Lal said this could effectively create a vacancy in the office of the Supervisor of Elections, which would be particularly problematic during an election period after the writ of elections had been issued.

He said the provision should instead require recusal from the particular decision.

CDD also strongly supported Clause 3, which proposes repealing sections 1B and 1C that allow the supervisor to compel information despite laws relating to confidentiality, privilege or secrecy.

Mr Lal described these powers as “dangerous”, saying they could allow the supervisor to override privacy laws and compel the seizure of private information, devices and documents.

He said CDD also recommended reviewing Section 6(1A) to ensure the remaining information-gathering power could not recreate the powers being removed.

item.title: ‘Don’t change rules before polls’
item.description: Parliament should avoid making significant changes to electoral laws within a year of an election. Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) chief executive officer Nilesh Lal made the submission to the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights as it considers four electoral Bills.
item.content:encoded:
Parliament should avoid making significant changes to electoral laws within a year of an election.

Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) chief executive officer Nilesh Lal made the submission to the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights as it considers four electoral Bills.

Mr Lal said the Bills presented Parliament with an opportunity for meaningful electoral reform but warned that the timing of changes was important to ensure stability and certainty in the electoral process.

“The Venice Commission’s code of good practice on electoral matters states that the fundamental elements of electoral law particularly the electoral system membership of electoral commissions and constituency boundaries should not normally be changed less than one year before an election,” Mr Lal said.

“Its interpretive guideline goes further and states more generally that electoral reforms intended to apply at an election should be sufficiently early to be genuinely implementable at that election.”

Mr Lal said the principle was particularly relevant as Fiji was now within the constitutional window for an election to be called, with the timing of the election ultimately determined by the Prime Minister.

He said the proposed changes covered areas including campaigning, polling, offences, counting, results and voter assistance.

While acknowledging that the Bills did not substantially change Fiji’s electoral formula or constituency boundaries, Mr Lal said Parliament should still consider the implications of changing the rules close to an election.

“Election officials needed time to develop procedures and train staff, while political parties, candidates, civil society, the media and voters needed clarity about the new rules.”

Mr Lal said voters needed confidence that electoral changes were not being made for short-term political convenience or political agendas.

He said electoral rules should be settled sufficiently early to allow all stakeholders to prepare for the election.

item.title: Call for clearer offence laws
item.description: PARLIAMENT should not amend a complicated criminal framework through fragmented textual substitution, Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) chief executive officer Nilesh Lal says. Making submissions to the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights on the proposed electoral Bills, Mr Lal said there was a drafting problem with proposed Section 135A because it applied to “any person”, wh
item.content:encoded:
PARLIAMENT should not amend a complicated criminal framework through fragmented textual substitution, Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD) chief executive officer Nilesh Lal says.

Making submissions to the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights on the proposed electoral Bills, Mr Lal said there was a drafting problem with proposed Section 135A because it applied to “any person”, which could include political parties and other legal entities.

He said the provision included imprisonment and automatic disqualification from the National Register of Voters.

“A political party cannot be imprisoned,” Mr Lal said.

“A company cannot be removed from the National Register of Voters because it was never a voter.”

He also questioned how proposed Section 135A would interact with existing Section 151, which already provides for electoral disqualification.

“Parliament should make clear how these regimes interact.”

Mr Lal said CDD recommended a consolidated offence schedule outlining prohibited conduct, required intention or knowledge, offence categories and penalties.

“This would provide greater clarity for citizens, candidates, political parties, the Fijian Elections Office, enforcement authorities and the courts.”

item.title: A new Kali Tui takes the stage
item.description: Kali Tui is treating VT1S 2026 like a reset. She says this year she’s bringing new songs and a bigger band to FMF Gymnasium this Saturday. She will perform more than eight songs. The main moment will be the first live performances of Tadra and Galala.
item.content:encoded:
Kali Tui is treating VT1S 2026 like a reset. She says this year she’s bringing new songs and a bigger band to FMF Gymnasium this Saturday.

She will perform more than eight songs. The main moment will be the first live performances of Tadra and Galala.

“I have new songs such as Tadra and Galala, which I haven’t performed on a big super stage,” she said.

The show will be semi-live, with DJ Unikk Kelly and Izzy on drums to push the festival vibe.

“It’s going to be a semi-live set. It’s going to be awesome. It’s going to be festival music,” she said.

This is her third year performing. She calls it her first time back as a more seasoned artist. She shares the night with Myshaan on his second Fiji appearance, plus DJ Drishant, the Room Core Gang and Young Blood.

“I’m excited to perform live on stage again as a new person.”

“To everybody who’s been supporting me since day one, thank you so much for the love, support and encouragement throughout my years and career here at the VT1s.”

Tickets are $30 GA and $100 VIP on Ticketmax.

The concert will be held this Saturday at the FMF Gymnasium with gates opening at 4pm and a total of 39 artists performing.

item.title: School teacher granted bail for rape
item.description: A schoolteacher accused of raping his student has been granted bail by the High Court in Suva. The accused appeared before Justice Daniel Goundar today, charged with one count of digital rape.
item.content:encoded:
A schoolteacher accused of raping his student has been granted bail by the High Court in Suva.

The accused appeared before Justice Daniel Goundar today, charged with one count of digital rape.

He is alleged to have raped a 16-year-old female student between June 1 and July 20 this year.

The State did not object to bail but sought strict and standard bail conditions, including a condition that the accused not interfere with State witnesses.

The matter was adjourned to September 21

item.title: Flu going around – Lalabalavu
item.description: INFLUENZA-LIKE illnesses (ILI) and acute respiratory infections (ARI) are affecting a large number of people across Fiji, with the Ministry of Health urging the public to take precautions and seek medical attention if symptoms worsen. Minister for Health Dr Atonio Lalabalavu said fever and cough were among the common symptoms, with the illness spreading easily among family members.
item.content:encoded:
INFLUENZA-LIKE illnesses (ILI) and acute respiratory infections (ARI) are affecting a large number of people across Fiji, with the Ministry of Health urging the public to take precautions and seek medical attention if symptoms worsen.

Minister for Health Dr Atonio Lalabalavu said fever and cough were among the common symptoms, with the illness spreading easily among family members.

“Overall, I can say with certainty there’s a flu going around and it’s really affecting a lot of people,” Dr Lalabalavu said.

He urged people with symptoms to drink plenty of fluids, rest and take Paracetamol to manage fever and discomfort.

“Our advice is to drink lots of water, have rest, take your Paracetamol, and if you have a feeling that you’re not improving, then go to the hospital to seek further assistance.

Dr Lalabalavu said the ministry routinely raised public awareness during flu outbreaks, advising people to keep warm, stay hydrated and seek medical attention early.

“Like with any flu outbreak or in the flu season, we usually put awareness out to the general public to keep warm, drink lots of fluid, and seek help and medical attention as early as possible.”

He urged the public to take precautions as the illness continues to spread.
